lead: Dry medical gas from a cylinder or pipeline holds almost no water. The airway lining needs water and heat; without them it crusts, bleeds and narrows. A humidifier adds water as vapour and never carries a drug. A nebulizer makes fine droplets and can carry a drug. An inhaler delivers a measured drug dose. These devices are used in oxygen therapy, asthma, COPD, intensive care and at home.
prereq: You need spirometry and lung volumes, and ventilator types and modes for the ventilator circuit.

sections.h3: Why dry gas hurts the airway

blocks.text: Normal breathing conditions air in the nose. By the time gas reaches the carina it is close to body temperature, 37 °C, and nearly saturated with water vapour. Saturated gas at 37 °C holds 44 mg of water per litre. Absolute humidity is the mass of water vapour in a litre of gas, written mg/L. The saturation value changes with temperature. The point in the airway where gas reaches 37 °C and full saturation is the isothermic saturation boundary. It sits below the carina in normal breathing. Dry oxygen moves this boundary deeper. The lower airway then gives up its own water and heat. Mucus thickens, cilia stop moving, and the patient may wheeze or bleed.

blocks.where: M<sub>w</sub> is water mass per minute (mg/min); AH is the absolute humidity of saturated gas at 37 °C (44 mg/L); Q is gas flow (L/min). For completely dry gas, the water to be added equals the full saturated value, AH = 44 mg/L. For partly humid gas, subtract the humidity already present before multiplying by Q.

blocks.text: Humidifiers add water as vapour. They do not put drug into the gas. A bubble-through humidifier passes gas through a bottle of sterile water; gas leaves with vapour. It is simple and cheap, but bubbling makes noise and the water path can become contaminated. A pass-over humidifier flows gas over a wet surface or wick and adds vapour without bubbling. A heated humidifier warms a chamber, often to 32–37 °C, so the gas can carry more water. A heated-wire circuit warms the tube to stop vapour condensing as rainout. The heater control uses a temperature sensor at the chamber or near the patient. A heat-and-moisture exchanger (HME), also called an artificial nose, traps heat and water from exhaled gas on a hydrophobic membrane or foam and returns some to the next breath. It needs no water supply and no power. It suits short transport or a patient whose upper airway is bypassed by an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy. It is not needed when the natural upper airway is working. It is not good for long ventilation with high humidity, thick secretions or low tidal volume, because it adds dead space and resistance. The worked example shows why a heated chamber must be refilled: 10 L/min of dry oxygen needs about 26 g of water each hour at full saturation.

Too much water is also a hazard. Rainout in the tubing can run into the patient or block the tube, wet flow sensors make the ventilator read wrong volumes, a chamber set above 37 °C can scald the airway, and small infants can take in too much water. A warm water reservoir also grows bacteria, so sterile water, closed refill systems and regular circuit changes are used.

Nebulizers make droplets, not just vapour, so they can carry a drug. A jet nebulizer uses compressed air or oxygen through a narrow venturi; the low pressure draws liquid up a tube, and a baffle breaks it into droplets. The mass median aerodynamic diameter (MMAD) is the droplet size at which half the mass is in smaller droplets. For lower-airway deposition, MMAD is usually 1–5 µm. Smaller droplets may be exhaled like a gas; larger droplets hit the mouth and throat. An ultrasonic nebulizer uses a piezoelectric crystal vibrating at high frequency to throw a fountain of fine droplets. It is quiet and needs no gas flow, but it can heat the liquid and is less useful for some drugs. A mesh nebulizer pushes liquid through a vibrating plate with tiny holes, giving fine droplets with low residual volume. Inhalers give a measured dose. A metered-dose inhaler (MDI) has a pressurised canister with drug and propellant; one press releases a fixed dose. A spacer holds the cloud so the patient can breathe it in slowly; it cuts drug deposited in the mouth and throat. A dry-powder inhaler (DPI) holds drug powder; the patient's breath breaks the powder into particles. It needs no propellant but needs enough inspiratory flow. Oxygen delivery devices: a nasal cannula gives low-flow oxygen through two prongs; a simple face mask gives a higher flow; a venturi mask uses a jet and air entrainment to give a fixed inspired oxygen fraction (FiO₂), such as 24%, 28% or 35%. Humidification is added when flow is high, when the gas is dry, or when the upper airway is bypassed.

figure.caption: Saturated gas holds more water as it warms: 23 mg/L at 25 °C and 44 mg/L at 37 °C. Dry oxygen at 10 L/min needs the full 44 mg/L, 26.4 g/h; room air at 50 % humidity already carries 11.5 mg/L, so it needs 32.5 mg/L, 19.5 g/h.

examples.question: A patient breathes 10 L/min of completely dry oxygen. Saturated gas at 37 °C holds 44 mg of water per litre. (a) How much water must be added per minute to saturate the gas? (b) How much per hour, in grams?
steps: Identify the flow Q = 10 L/min and the final absolute humidity AH = 44 mg/L.
Water per minute = AH × Q = 44 mg/L × 10 L/min = 440 mg/min.
Water per hour = 440 mg/min × 60 min/h = 26,400 mg/h.
Convert milligrams to grams: 26,400 mg ÷ 1000 mg/g = 26.4 g/h.
examples.answer: The gas needs 440 mg of water per minute, which is 26.4 g per hour.
examples.check:
q = 10
ah = 44
per_min = ah * q
per_hour = per_min * 60 / 1000
print(per_min)
print(per_hour)

examples.question: Room air at 25 °C and 50 % relative humidity is given to a patient at 10 L/min through a tracheostomy, so the nose does not condition it. Saturated air at 25 °C holds 23 mg/L and at 37 °C 44 mg/L. Find the water already present, the water the humidifier must add per minute and the water used per hour.
steps: Deficit to reach saturation at 37 °C = 44 − 11.5 = 32.5 mg/L.
Water to add per minute = 32.5 mg/L × 10 L/min = 325 mg/min.
Per hour = 325 × 60 = 19,500 mg = 19.5 g/h, against 26.4 g/h for the same flow of completely dry oxygen.
examples.answer: The air already carries 11.5 mg/L, so the humidifier adds 325 mg/min, which is 19.5 g of water per hour.

traps: A humidifier and a nebulizer are not the same: a humidifier adds vapour and never a drug; a nebulizer makes droplets and can carry a drug.
Bigger droplets do not go deeper. Above about 5 µm, droplets settle in the upper airway and mouth.
The 44 mg/L figure is for saturated gas at 37 °C, not for room-temperature water or room air.
In the water-rate sum, match minutes with minutes or hours with hours. Multiplying mg/min by 60 gives mg/h, not g/h until you divide by 1000.
An HME is not a heated humidifier. It recycles exhaled heat and water and has no water chamber.

quiz.q: State the absolute humidity of saturated gas at 37 °C.
quiz.a: 44 mg of water per litre of gas.

quiz.q: Give one clear difference between a humidifier and a nebulizer.
quiz.a: A humidifier adds water vapour and does not carry a drug. A nebulizer makes liquid droplets and can carry a drug into the airway.

quiz.q: What is MMAD, and what range is used for lower-airway deposition?
quiz.a: MMAD is the mass median aerodynamic diameter: the droplet size at which half the mass is in smaller droplets. For lower-airway deposition the usual range is 1–5 µm.

quiz.q: A patient gets 8 L/min of dry oxygen. Using 44 mg/L for saturated gas at 37 °C, find the water needed per hour in grams.
How does a venturi mask give a fixed FiO₂?
quiz.a: A jet of oxygen entrains a known amount of room air through ports. The jet size and air ports set the oxygen fraction, for example 24%, 28% or 35%.

quiz.q: Why is an HME a poor choice for long ventilation when secretions are thick?
quiz.a: An HME adds dead space and resistance. It returns only part of the exhaled heat and water, so it may not give enough humidification for thick secretions. A heated humidifier is better when high humidity is needed.

quiz.q: Why does a spacer reduce drug deposited in the mouth from an MDI?
quiz.a: The spacer slows the aerosol cloud and lets propellant evaporate. The patient inhales slowly, so fewer large particles hit the mouth and throat and more small particles reach the airway.

quiz.q: Name the three common types of nebulizer.
A venturi mask is to give 28 % oxygen. Find the ratio of entrained air to oxygen, and the total flow when the oxygen flow is 4 L/min.
quiz.a: Let the oxygen flow be 1 and the air flow A. Then (1 + 0.21 A) ÷ (1 + A) = 0.28, so 0.72 = 0.07 A and A = 10.3. With 4 L/min of oxygen the air flow is 4 × 10.3 = 41.1 L/min and the total is 45.1 L/min, more than the patient's peak inspiratory flow, so the FiO₂ stays fixed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern practice uses vibrating-mesh nebulizers for portable therapy and heated high-flow nasal cannula for oxygen with better humidity control. Smart inhalers add dose counters and Bluetooth logging to check adherence. Drug-particle engineering aims to tune MMAD for specific lung regions. Search for heated humidifier rainout, mesh nebulizer residual volume, and inhaler spacer technique.
